notes.title: Note 1
notes.text:
Since housing is a fundamental need for people, some people suggest that it should be free to those who are unable to afford it. Personally, I do not agree with this school of thought.

Some argue that housing serves as a haven for self-healing at the end of the day. Parents may confront challenges at work, while their offspring also experience the same at school, all of which may sap both their physical and mental energy and thus require recovery. Gathering at the same place is believed to provide a cosy atmosphere and warm moments to express a sense of anxiety, discomfort, and fear they face and receive love, empathy, and encouragement. Without a place of belonging, people may experience repeated negative emotions every night, while living and sleeping in strange places regularly may cause people to be exposed to thieves or criminals. This, as a result, sincerely calls for support for free housing for individuals who cannot afford it, with the aim of improving their lives at a basic level.

Although this call appears to be reasonable, I assume that whether the national budget is adequate and whether groups of people outside the beneficiary group are willing to pay more taxes in support of others are important considerations. Building a house, even a very small or decrepit house, requires substantial investment, as the government may pay for materials, construction workers, electricity networks, and water supplies. The total cost for a single house thus requires additional tax payments from citizens. However, some may oppose this idea since they believe that they do not receive any benefits from this investment. Also, in developing nations, the government must allocate financial resources to economic development, environmental problems, or education and healthcare, which may impose a financial burden on the government if it must take on the responsibility of providing free housing. Chief among these concerns are ethical concerns. The government may find it difficult to distinguish those who genuinely cannot afford it from those who use fraudulent tactics only to receive free housing. Were this to happen, social disparity may be widened, in which people who are inherently rich become richer, while those who suffer from housing scarcity may be pushed into further impoverished circumstances.

In conclusion, the idea of providing free housing to those who cannot pay for it sounds reasonable, but I believe that this is impractical. A series of free housing units cannot be built immediately just because people think it is a basic need; in practice, it involves a wide range of factors: unsolved domestic issues, a constrained national budget, the willingness of citizens to pay more taxes, and moral concerns. I contend that the government may support individuals by allowing them to take out loans with low interest rates or renting accommodation at a lower cost. A house is more than bricks and walls; it is where a sense of belonging takes root and sentimental bonds are woven, but it is by no means the only answer.
